summary.text: A constellation is an area of the celestial sphere containing a group of visible stars that form a perceived pattern, often an animal, a mythological subject or an object.
People used constellations to tell stories of their beliefs and mythology, and naming them also helped astronomers and navigators identify stars more easily.
In 1922 the International Astronomical Union accepted the modern list of 88 constellations, and in 1928 it adopted boundaries that cover the entire celestial sphere.

facts.label: Official total
facts.value: 88 constellations, each with a Latin name

facts.label: Ptolemy's list
facts.value: 48 traditional constellations, listed in the Almagest

facts.label: Official boundaries
facts.value: Adopted in 1928, covering the entire celestial sphere

facts.label: Southern additions
facts.value: Added from the 15th century to the mid-18th century

facts.value: Familiar outlines become unrecognizable after tens of thousands of years or more

items.prompt: From where you live, one group of stars circles all night and never dips below the horizon. What is such a constellation called?

options.label: Equatorial
Zodiacal
Circumpolar
Asterism

items.explain: A constellation or star that never sets below the horizon from a particular latitude is termed circumpolar.

items.prompt: Two stars sit close together in a constellation's outline. Are they necessarily close together in space?

options.label: No, they usually lie at a variety of distances from Earth
Yes, stars in the same outline are neighbours
Yes, but only for the brightest stars
No, they are always on opposite sides of the galaxy

items.explain: Stars in constellations can appear near each other in the sky, but they usually lie at a variety of distances away from the Earth.

items.prompt: Many cultures invented their own constellations, yet only 88 appear on today's official list. What best explains this?

options.label: The other cultures' stars were not visible to astronomers
Only one set was internationally recognized after many were invented
The other patterns were too faint for anyone to trace
Older constellations were deleted because they were wrong

items.explain: Different cultures invented their own constellations, and the IAU formally accepted the modern list of 88.

items.prompt: Observers use the Big Dipper to navigate the night sky, but it is not a constellation by the formal definition. What is it?

options.label: A zodiac sign lying along the ecliptic
A Flamsteed designation for a single star
A circumpolar region of the sky
An asterism within the constellation Ursa Major

items.explain: Asterisms are star patterns that are not constellations under the formal definition; the Big Dipper is in the constellation of Ursa Major.

items.prompt: The stars you see in the evening sky shift as the months pass. Why?

options.label: The stars themselves travel around the Sun each year
Earth's axial tilt switches direction every month
Night falls on different parts of Earth's orbit as the year goes on
The stars burn out and reappear in new places

items.explain: Constellation positions change through the year because night on Earth occurs at gradually different portions of its orbit around the Sun.

items.prompt: Why were constellations in the far southern sky added from the 15th century onward?

options.label: Ptolemy ordered the southern sky to be mapped
European explorers began traveling to the Southern Hemisphere
The southern stars had only just formed
The IAU needed more constellations to reach 88

items.explain: Constellations in the far southern sky were added from the 15th century until the mid-18th century, when European explorers began traveling to the Southern Hemisphere.
